title: Stranger Things: Upside Down - IP games are good now, actually.
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IQ3zeRLgnt4

Daniel (@dungeondive) uses CMON's Stranger Things: Upside Down, designed by Rob Daviau, to argue a thesis: licensed games are good now. In the Toys R Us era a board game of your favourite show was garbage nine times out of ten. This one he files near Horrified — not quite as good, but a genuine gateway.

He's candid about the show first. The eighties texture, Winona Ryder, and the opening premise of kids playing D&D in a basement all land; he thinks the writers stopped knowing what to do with Eleven and Mike after season one, and that anything with Steve, Dustin, Robin or Erica is gold.

The game covers seasons one and two on a double-sided board — Hawkins above, the tunnels beneath — which he calls one of the coolest boards he's seen, praising the painted art specifically for not being show stills. Underneath it's threat management: stacks of mostly-hidden challenge tokens cleared by spending action cards, fear standing in for hit points, and hazard icons on those cards dictating how many scene cards bite back. His best structural note is that banking safe turns leaves you eventually holding a hand of pure hazard — a fair imitation of dramatic tension.

Four gripes: no group movement, no trading items, no dice at all where a small press-your-luck die would help, and too few items and allies to stay fresh.

----

Daniel wants a press-your-luck die added to a purely card-driven system. Does a little randomness make a co-op better, or just longer?
